Coordinated issuance and connected-pool correction
30 September 2026. Reproducible hypothetical market experiment.
Question and scope
Can a controller with no initial destination treasury assets use renewed, accepted source claims to
acquire pDAI and induce profitable correction through connected pools? Yes, in this constructed market.
The experiment grants the source issuance and representation premises and tests their market
consequences. It neither deploys those capabilities nor establishes them on PulseChain.
The earlier standing-facility experiment (Appendix 60) tests a fixed-inventory comparator. Its exhaustion
result does not by itself evaluate a network that continually introduces accepted source assets. This
experiment gives that network its proposed additional input and tracks where the resulting inventory
goes.
Method
Four constant-product pools charge 0.3% of input; fees remain inside reserves. D denotes pDAI, P PLS, U a
surrounding fungible asset, and X an accepted destination representation of a source asset or receipt. No
backing valuation or guaranteed dollar price is assigned to X. U begins at a one-dollar marginal PLS price
but has no independent redemption promise. This makes propagation of pressure into surrounding
assets visible.
Pool Initial reserves
X/U 10,000,000 X and 10,000,000 U
D/U 10,000,000 D and 10,000,000 U
D/P 1,000,000 D and 10,000,000,000 P
U/P 10,000,000 U and 100,000,000,000 P
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 177

The fixed external reference is $0.0001 per PLS. Controller balances start at zero. Outside traders hold
the amounts needed for their specified shocks; the arbitrageur has owned PLS capital. These are existing
assets, not assets created by the controller. LP ownership and withdrawals are not simulated.
For input q, input reserve x, output reserve y and fee f, the pool pays y(1−f)q / [x+(1−f)q], then adds the
entire input and subtracts the output. All amounts use Decimal precision 60. No floating-point numbers
enter the model.
For a sale shock, the controller issues source X, locks it and receives one destination X per locked source
unit. It sells X → U → D, retaining D. A separate trader chooses the more profitable of P → D → U → P and its
reverse, optimizes trade size up to its budget, and acts only if gross profit exceeds 3,000 PLS gas. A
binary search selects controller input sufficient to restore the D/P marginal price to at least $0.995 after
that correction, within a per-round issuance limit of one trillion X.
For a buy shock, the controller sells retained D into D/U. The trader's reverse cycle can then lower D/P
toward $1.005. The controller never mints D in this experiment. Insufficient D inventory therefore
remains a meaningful test.
Each round assumes that any required bridge delivery has completed. The model does not shorten a
challenge window. Controller gas, bridge fees and losses during latency are excluded, so this is a gross
capacity experiment, not a net profit forecast. Only arbitrageur profit includes the stated gas charge.
End-to-end results
An outside sale of 200,000 D receives 1,662,497,915.624479 PLS and moves the instantaneous
marginal price from $1 to $0.694792. The original seller's average execution is about $0.831249; later
correction does not change that payment.
The controller issues and bridges 458,545.820869 X, receives 437,183.459185 U, and buys 
417,666.978491 D. The trader starts its corrective cycle with 1,642,425,206.936962 PLS, earning 
404,756,426.740876 PLS after the assumed gas charge. D/P reaches $0.995.
The controller has acquired more D than the outside seller supplied because it also acquired inventory
previously held by pools. No tokens are missing: source issuance equals source escrow and newly issued
destination X, while every non-X token is conserved across all destination accounts.
Next, an outside buyer spends 2 billion PLS, receiving 167,029.366446 D, and raises the marginal
price to $1.433043. The controller sells 354,543.328273 D into D/U, receiving 356,785.113193 U.
The reverse arbitrage earns 367,247,096.815829 PLS after modeled gas and lowers D/P to $1.005.
The controller ends with 63,123.650218 D and 356,785.113193 U.
These retained assets are holdings, not a demonstrated net profit. The X claim and the resulting risk held
by its purchasers remain part of the consolidated account. No X redemption liability is silently settled or
assigned a zero cost.
A fourth scenario extends this sequence with another 200,000-D sale. The controller reuses the 
356,785.113193 U recovered during buying, adds 106,688.977595 newly issued X through X/U,
and acquires another 429,624.257935 D. Corrective arbitrage again returns D/P to $0.995. This
demonstrates reinvestment of recovered inventory. It is distinct from earning new outside fees, which
this model does not allocate to treasury ownership.
Repeated selling and renewal
Eight consecutive 200,000-D sales are each corrected to $0.995 in this model. The controller
accumulates 3,265,728.565660 D, issuing a cumulative 6,769,533.095641 X. The last correction
requires 1,512,055.592012 X, compared with 458,545.820869 X initially.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 178

This is a successful repeated intervention under the chosen assumptions, with a measurable transfer of
exposure. X/U now holds 16,769,533.095641 X and 5,972,141.013973 U, instead of 10 million of
each. U/P's marginal dollar price falls to $0.694741. The controller has maintained the chosen pDAI
price by changing the surrounding network; it has not kept every asset at $1.
This distinction matters for a design that expects FRAX, pUSDC, pUSDT and other assets to support one
another. If each must also retain a dollar reference, their own corrective sources and final output
inventories need to be specified. Internal parity alone leaves the common dollar price undetermined.
Additional bridges can add accepted inputs or reach additional reserves; their existence does not, by
itself, establish replenishment of every spent output asset.
For a constant-product X/U pool, ignoring fees for the bound, finite input gives U_out = R_U X_in/(R_X+X_in)
< R_U. Renewing X can continue purchases while conversion remains available, but cannot extract more U
than the pool owns without incoming U. A network can refill a particular pool from another; the
consolidated account must identify where that U originated and who now holds X.
Inventory asymmetry
A separate buying shock begins before any controller accumulation. Market arbitrage lowers D/P from
$1.439280 to $1.065651, but cannot attain the specified upper target. The controller has no D to sell.
This case demonstrates the need for prior inventory or an additional exact-D delivery route. It does not
test every possible network: authorized D issuance, releasable D escrow or available lending would be
additional explicit capabilities with their own balances and obligations.
Reflexivity and LP accounting
The experiment models accumulation directly. It does not model ownership of LP shares, reinvestment,
endogenous confidence or borrower demand. Those channels are accounted for in the accumulation
study (Appendix 65): outside fees and interest can replenish controlled assets after costs, whereas
internal transfers do not create consolidated earnings.
The same swap equations apply whether withdrawable LP shares are held by the operator, outside
holders or an inaccessible address. Those arrangements differ in who can withdraw principal and realize
fees. Irrecoverably held shares can prevent the corresponding liquidity withdrawal; swaps still alter the
reserves. Thus burned LP ownership does not supply a fixed reserve composition or a spendable fee
claim for the controller.
Reproduction and validation
Run from the repository root, selecting a fresh output path:
python Research/scripts/model_pulsechain_coordinated_network.py \
  --manifest Research/experiments/pulsechain_coordinated_network_20260930.json \
  --output artifacts/pulsechain-coordinated-mechanism-20260930/network-results.json
The saved output records manifest and script hashes, assumptions, each shock, controller input,
arbitrage route and profit, pool reserves, treasury inventory, and conservation residuals. Its maximum
per-token conservation residual is below 1e-35 units; the observed maximum is 1e-48 across these
scenarios. Source issuance, escrow and destination issuance match exactly in Decimal accounting.
Source and destination claims are kept separate rather than counted as two independent assets.
Outputs are reproducible byte for byte.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 179

An independent 90-digit replay gives a maximum pool-reserve difference below 4e-49 units. Writing a
complete cycle as Aq/(B+Cq) gives the unconstrained profit-maximizing input (sqrt(A B)−B)/C, clipped to
zero and the trader's budget. The numerical optimizer's inputs differ from this closed-form solution by
less than 0.000003 PLS across the tested cycles. The independent replay uses no imports from the model
script. Results are recorded in artifacts/pulsechain-coordinated-mechanism-20260930/validation.json.
The optimizer uses the concavity of compositions of positive constant-product swap curves. The
validation checks the closed-form cycle optimum independently, all token conservation identities, both
directional effects, eight renewed corrections, the unsatisfied inventory case and original seller
execution. It tests a declared mechanism, not live profitability or perfect stability.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 180
